Chapter Two: The Sudden Fall and the Beginning of Captivity
Picture this—one ordinary day, everything changes. The father of the family, a man everyone respected, suddenly finds himself accused of being part of a failed coup against the king. It’s not a dramatic explosion, but more like a shadow slowly creeping in. What used to be a safe haven—the palace—now feels like a cage. Guards start appearing at the gates, and instead of being called to a celebration, the family is summoned for questioning.
The children, wide-eyed and scared, cling to their mother as soldiers search every corner of their home. The father is led away, leaving the family stuck in a painful limbo. They’re watched, questioned, cut off from everyone they know. Their mother tries to keep up appearances, pushing for routines and manners, but the worry in her eyes tells a different story.
Before long, they’re moved out of their home—sent from place to place, each one more dismal than the last. At first, it’s a comfortable villa, but it might as well be a prison. Every move is monitored, every word overheard. The children, who once played freely in the palace gardens, now find themselves trapped in tiny rooms. Their world just keeps getting smaller.
Days blur into weeks, and weeks into months. The family hears nothing about their father’s fate. Rumors swirl—executions, betrayals—each one heavier than the last. Their mother, once their rock, is fighting to hold everyone together. She invents games, tells stories, and tries her best to keep hope alive, but the strain is always there, just beneath the surface.
Then comes another move—this time, to a remote prison in the desert. The journey is long and frightening, with guards barking orders, and the children huddling together for comfort. When they arrive, it’s worse than they could have imagined: a windowless compound, surrounded by endless sand, with heat and fear thick in the air. They’re completely cut off—no news, no friends, no hope from the outside world.
In those first days of captivity, the family clings to what they have: each other. The mother becomes both protector and teacher, doing everything she can to shield her children from despair. The eldest daughter, now stepping into adulthood far too soon, helps care for her younger siblings and tries to keep their spirits up. Their world has shrunk to a handful of small rooms, but inside those walls, they find ways to survive—through stories, through songs, and sometimes just by holding hands in the dark.
It doesn’t take long to realize: survival here isn’t just about getting through each day. It’s about finding meaning in even the smallest moments. The family learns to adapt—to find comfort in the tiniest routines, and to draw strength from each other. Even though the outside world seems to have forgotten them, they manage to build a world of their own—a world held together by love, by memory, and by their stubborn refusal to let go of hope.
